_: The one place PocketAgent's colour and icon geometry are written down. tools/make_brand.py reads this and emits every derived asset; tests/brand-assets-test.py reads it and refuses anything that drifted. Editing a colour here and running the generator is the whole procedure -- there is no second place to remember.

brand._: A dark tile, bone brackets, and one violet spark. The ground is near-black so the icon sits with the app's own interior and with the phones these agents are actually used on; the colour moves off the tile and into the mark, which is where the eye goes. Violet was settled by putting the mark beside the four agents this app hosts, at launcher size: Codex and Cursor are dark tiles with pale marks, Claude is terracotta, Antigravity's arch is a multicolour rainbow. A violet spark is the one thing none of them has -- and it stays clear of the three colours that mean something inside the app.

neutral._: Warm, not grey. The interface is deliberately neutral: buttons and links are ink on cream and bone on ink, so that every coloured pixel in the app is carrying meaning rather than decoration.

semantic._: The only other colours in the app, and each one means exactly one thing.

geometry._: The mark on a 512 artboard: two brackets around a four-point spark. Every derived size is this artboard scaled, so proportions never drift between the launcher, the splash and the notification. The stroke is 38 and the spark's control offset 19 because at 48 px -- the smallest a launcher draws -- a 34 stroke went spindly and a 15 offset collapsed the spark into a dot.

desktop._: The Ubuntu desktop inside the container is part of the same product, so its chrome carries the brand's hue. The rule is stated here and enforced by tests/brand-assets-test.py as a positive requirement rather than a blacklist: every colour in the desktop scripts must sit within hue_tolerance of the brand hue, or be near-neutral. A blacklist goes stale the moment the brand changes; this does not. The one exception is the terminal's ANSI palette, which every program on the system depends on and is not ours to re-tint. Reds and ambers are the exception the other way: they are status in the desktop's chrome exactly as they are in the app, so status_hue_bands names them rather than letting any far-off hue slip through on a distance rule.
